messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 66

Michael is forty-five years old, a journalist, and he speaks about his work the way a soldier might speak about a war he is still fighting. He has been married to his wife, Claire, for eighteen years, and he tells me this fact as if it is a piece of evidence he is presenting in his own defense. He sits forward in the chair, his hands wrapped around his knees, and he does not lean back.

He was in Syria for six weeks, embedded with a unit of opposition fighters. He had done this kind of work for two decades—Kosovo, Iraq, Afghanistan. He knew the calculus of risk, the arithmetic of danger. He tells me that he always believed he could talk his way out of anything, that his press credentials were a kind of armor. That belief lasted until the checkpoint outside of Raqqa, when the men in mismatched uniforms pulled him from the car and put a bag over his head.

He was held for forty-seven days. He tells me the number without hesitation, as if he has counted them many times. The first week was the worst, he says, not because of the beatings, which came later, but because of the uncertainty. He did not know if anyone was looking for him. He did not know if his network had already declared him dead. He was kept in a room with no windows, a concrete floor, a single lightbulb that never turned off. He learned to sleep with his eyes open, or rather, he learned to stop sleeping altogether.

The interrogations were repetitive. They asked him the same questions in different orders: Who do you work for? Why are you here? Who sent you? He gave them the same answers, over and over, until his voice became a mechanical thing, a recording. He learned to dissociate during the interrogations, to watch himself from a corner of the ceiling. He tells me that he still does this, sometimes, in his living room.

He was released in a prisoner exchange. He does not remember the handover, only the sensation of being passed from one set of hands to another, like a package. When he landed back in the United States, his editor met him at the airport. Claire was there too. He hugged her, but he says he could not feel her arms around him. He felt like he was watching a movie of himself embracing his wife.

That was three years ago. He returned to work after six months, because he did not know what else to do. He covers city council meetings now, zoning disputes, school board elections. He calls it "the kiddie table." His editor thinks he is doing well. He files his stories on time. He does not miss deadlines. But he cannot write about violence anymore. He tried, once, to cover a protest that turned into a riot, and he had to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he sat on the floor for forty minutes, his hands over his ears.

He is hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. He scans every room for exits. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He cannot tolerate being in crowds, but he also cannot tolerate being alone. He and Claire have not slept in the same bed for two years, because he thrashes and shouts in his sleep. He tells me that he dreams of the lightbulb, the one that never turned off. He dreams that he is still in the room, and that no one has come for him.

He drinks more than he should. He knows this. He tells me that he does not want to talk about his feelings, because he does not trust feelings. He trusts facts. He trusts the byline at the top of his article. He does not trust the man who was in that room, the one who learned to leave his own body. He says he does not know that man. He says he does not want to know him.
